name: Lars Lofgren
sum: Base your 2027 SEO and GEO budget on which of 3 performance buckets your site is in.
text:
If you're deciding how to allocate your SEO/GEO budget for 2027, I'd base it on which of the 3 buckets that your site currently falls into (based on your 2026 performance).

I've had the fortune of working on a bunch of epic domains in the past few years. Huge brands, monster DRs, endless traffic, major budgets. Even in this cohort, SEO performance varies a lot. I have my suspicions for what causes this difference but that's another post for another time.

Roughly, every program has ended up in 1 of 3 buckets.

1) Google loves you = changes occur in weeks. New blog posts, updates, landing pages, technical fixes, whatever. In a lot of cases, you can see the impact in days. And it's not hard to show program progress over weeks. If this is you, go double down on whatever it is you're doing. I would, however, be careful about overspending on SEO. Somewhere in the $30-50K/month range is where I settle these days. After that, I spend on other channels. Increasing your budget from $10 to $20K? Definitely. Going from $50K to $100K? I probably wouldn't, even if things are going well. Overweighting on SEO can destroy the program.

2) Google likes you, doesn't love you though. Most changes take months to show real progress. You can definitely see progress YoY but nothing is a given. If this is you, I'd get your SEO budget into the $10-20K/month range at least. Take it seriously, keep building.

3) Google hates you. Feels like nothing ever works. If you squint, you can maybe see YoY progress but it all feels like a slog. Very common for sites that overweighted on SEO in the past (this is possible even for major brands). SEO got you into this mess, SEO will not get you out. For anyone in this bucket, I'd slash SEO budget to the bone. Maybe keep $5K/month for cleanup and basic updates. Cut everything else. Instead, dump all your budget into building other channels out (YouTube, Reddit, personal social profiles, etc). Ironically, this will make SEO a lot easier in the future.

DM me if you want a second set of eyes on your marketing budget. I can share a few quick thoughts with you directly (I always keep things private too). | 22 comments on LinkedIn

Google is testing removing AI Mode from search because AI ads make less money for advertisers.

Google’s also testing removing the Ask Anything box under AI Overviews… and removing AI Mode from their homepage.

Google has literally said AI Mode ads make everybody less money than traditional search ads: makes less money for Google, makes less money for advertisers.

In fact, this study about ChatGPT ads was just released- ChatGPT ads are terribly unprofitable.

"A ChatGPT ad click is worth $0.26. One of the largest publicly known accounts paid $1.72, more than six times as much.

Visitors from ChatGPT ads perform worse behind Google Ads, Google search, direct traffic, ChatGPT's own unpaid recommendations."

Just like Google's AI Mode ads, ChatGPT ads make advertisers less money.

Back in May this year, Google announced all these AI features at Google I/O.

Here's TechCrunch saying “The era of 10 blue links is officially over.”

People have been screaming SEO is dead for decades.

Next time you see a big hyped-up statement like this, my advice is to keep calm and to focus on the SEO that matters.

As long as there's large amounts of unorganized data to sort through, companies, people will always need search engine optimization.

Don't give into the hype. | 56 comments on LinkedIn

name: Malte Landwehr
sum: ChatGPT Business Hub is a worse GSC: real data, but few clicks, no prompts and an odd definition of a mention.
text:
My thoughts on the ChatGPT Business Hub: a worse GSC.

But also more than GSC. It includes functionality similar to Google Merchant Center and Google Business Profile.

The big plus? „Real“ data. Finally!

The big minus? No prompts, very generic topics, limited historical data, and a weird definition of what a mention is.

Also, very few clicks! But that is as expected.

Weird definition of mentions? Hear me out. Your brand is mentioned with a link to your website? That’s a mention! Your website is cited? That is a mention too - even if your brand was not mentioned in the answer at all.

Your brand is mention without a link? Or the link goes to your LinkedIn profile? Those are not mentions. 

There is also no differentiation between branded and unbranded prompts.

In the end, it has the purpose to convince you to give OpenAI access to all your data. It will not help you gain more citations, understand how you perform vs competitors, are help you be recommended more often.

Similar to Google Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools, it is a data source. It has value. But it is only one of multiple data points that should inform your execution layer and success measurement.

More details in the Peec AI blog. | 53 comments on LinkedIn

name: Nate Elliott
sum: Google Search has the same monthly users as in 2023. AI is not killing search.
text:
As Anthropic prepares to go public, this is your regular reminder that AI isn't killing search. It's not even making a dent.

Much of Anthropic's narrative rightly focuses on its strength as an enterprise tool. But Claude is also one of the world's largest chatbots, having separated itself this year from competitors like Perplexity and Grok.

Anthropic is likely to be valued at well over $1 trillion, and OpenAI is seeking a similar valuation next year. The main argument for such lofty numbers is that their chatbots will ravage the search industry: that people will stop using traditional discovery channels like Google, and that this will lead to a bonanza of subscription and advertising revenue for AI platforms.

But Google Search has the same number of monthly users now as it did in 2023. And the average Google Search user actually visits slightly more often now than in 2023.

So yes, billions of people around the world use AI on a regular basis. Yes, AI is changing the way many people search, and what they expect responses to look like. And yes, now that Google has gotten people using AI Overviews and AI Mode (which are part of the data in this chart), it needs to figure out how to better monetize these tools.

But no, chatbots are not killing search. Not even close. | 70 comments on LinkedIn

name: Dorcas Adisa
sum: A new site got 1K+ impressions in 4 days with no promotion. She lists the setup steps.
text:
As part of my AEO/GEO/SEO research, I built a website from scratch to see how quickly a new website could gain organic search visibility.

4 days after hosting the site, I'm already at 1K+ impressions. I haven't promoted the site or put the link anywhere online.




I didn't get here by luck though, I put some structure in place while building the website:

1.) Started by defining my new positioning. In my past life, I was Dorcas the content writer. Now, I am becoming an organic and AI search strategist and everything on my website (and LinkedIn) has to reflect that

2.) I used my new positioning to do keyword research and mapped out my website pages. My homepage targets a specific keyword, and each service I offer got its dedicated page and keyword focus. 


3.) I built a solid seo technical foundation to make the website accessible to search engines and AI crawlers. 

Some of the things I checked:
    - Minimized JavaScript on website, so important content is accessible
    - Ensure robot.txt allows AI search crawlers
    - Indexed all pages on GSC and Bing and checked that they're discoverable
    - Internally linked important pages so they're discoverable
    - Updated XML sitemaps so everything exists and everything is accessible

I'm still building, so this is quite interesting. I want to see what I can achieve in the next month. | 58 comments on LinkedIn

name: Jimmy Park
sum: Stop chasing high-volume prompts. In 1,455 repeat prompts, the same brands came back only 7.49% of the time.
text:
AI search is NOT the same as SEO. I don't care about keywords or search volume. Instead, I look at AEO Determinants.

Before:
- Upload highest-volume visibility prompts into a tracker
- Read whichever citations come back
- Write articles chasing them
- Hope you’re now cited

This is NOT the right way to do AEO.

Instead of trying to show up for prompts, you need to intercept Determinants. 

Explained:

1. Don't chase high-volume visibility prompts
- Prompts are long-tail. Two buyers rarely type the same thing.
- There's no reliable way to measure prompt volume.
- Tracked prompts don't recommend the same brands consistently. We ran 1,455 prompts back to back across 14 industries, and the same set of brands came back only 7.49% of the time.

2. Instead, chase determinants that appear consistently
- A Determinant is a factor the model weighs before it makes a recommendation.
- We measured more than 659,000 AI responses to buying prompts. In 94.4% of ChatGPT's answers, 2 or more of 5 Determinants show up together:

a) Audience (59.8% of answers) - who's asking, by role, company size, and situation.
b) Use case (92.5%) - the job, plus what they already run and where they're based.
c) Selection criteria (83.9%) - price, features, quality, support, compliance.
d) Credibility (55.6%) - reviews, studies, certifications, expert mentions.
e) Brand association (at least 17.1%) - how tightly the model links you to the category.

- For example, I asked ChatGPT "My TV is getting old. Which one should I buy?" It then asked me about my budget & screen size (selection criteria), what I watch & how bright the room is (use case) before it recommended a solution.

3. How to take advantage of Determinants

a) Map the Determinants for your category
- Run buying prompts through ChatGPT and note every question it asks before it recommends.
- Sort each question into a Determinant. For example, a question about role or company size is audience.

b) Adjust your own pages for audience, use case, and selection criteria
- Imagine you run AEO for a payroll tool.
- For Audience, you would name every buyer type on your pages. Founders, HR managers, and accountants, from 3 employees to 3,000.
- For Use Case, you would write a section for each situation a buyer is in, then answer it. Think hiring in a second state or paying contractors.
- For Selection Criteria, you would publish what buyers compare you on. Think price per employee, whether tax filing is included, and how support works.

Tobias (Loud & Lexis) I have been working on this together. We’ve analyzed 659k+ AI responses and with all our findings, have published the Determinants Manifesto. 

LINK: https://lnkd.in/gFqTeMhu | 61 comments on LinkedIn

name: Alex Groberman
sum: What Metehan Yesilyurt found about how Google's AI search picks the sites it recommends.
text:
Google accidentally revealed how its AI search systems choose which sites to recommend and send traffic to.

Now that none of it is much of a secret anymore, let’s talk about it.
With the new Google Search rolling out as we speak, it has never been more important to understand how to maximize value from this marketing channel.

If you want to see where your site stands across Google, ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity and broader AI search, you can do so for free here:

https://lnkd.in/gRaXKJxi

Let’s start from the beginning.

Metehan Yesilyurt, who previously went viral for his analysis of Perplexity’s ranking factors, recently broke down Google AI ranking factors in a fascinating blog post.

A lot of what he found also lines up with what SEO Stuff (seo-stuff.com) has been doing all year to get customers more traffic and sales.

Specifically with the done-for-you package:

https://lnkd.in/eZk7VPxz

Basically, Google sells much of the underlying retrieval infrastructure through Google Cloud Discovery Engine, also called Vertex AI Search.
By analyzing what Discovery Engine exposes, Yesilyurt was able to show how Google’s AI retrieval and ranking stack works.

The seven major signals he identified were Base Ranking, Gecko embedding similarity, Jetstream cross-attention relevance, BM25 keyword matching, predicted click-through rate, freshness and Boost/Bury rules.

In simpler terms, Google is combining traditional ranking signals with semantic similarity, deeper contextual relevance, keyword matching, engagement predictions, recency and manual business logic.

Discovery Engine exposes a maximum chunk size of 500 tokens, roughly 375 words, while ancestor headings can travel with each chunk and tables, images and page layouts can all be parsed with Gemini-enhanced understanding.

That means important ideas need to make sense inside relatively small, clearly labeled sections.

If your content is one massive wall of text, Google has a much harder job extracting the exact information it needs.

This is also why I keep talking about question-based headings, direct answers, clear comparisons and structured pages.

Additionally, Discovery Engine shows Google processing structured data using separate Searchable, Indexable and Retrievable settings.
Those can affect whether information can be found, used for filtering or ordering and surfaced by the model. Mind you, they are independent.

So a field can potentially influence retrieval or ranking without necessarily being displayed in exactly the same way.

That gives us a pretty significant clue about why structured data continues to matter as Google becomes more AI-driven.

Discovery Engine also reveals a four-stage pipeline: Prepare, Retrieve, Signal and Serve.
